claims.sentence: Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to take very detailed pictures from almost every angle.
claims.evidence: Retrieved text says a strong magnet lines up protons and radio wave bursts make them emit signals the scanner measures to build images; 'very detailed ... from almost every angle' not found.
claims.newSentence: MRI uses a strong magnet and radio waves to build images of the inside of the body.

claims.sentence: It does not use X-rays or other ionising radiation.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: 'Unlike CT or X-ray, no ionizing radiation is used in MRI' (US wording); NHS Inform says it does not use X-rays and is not linked to increased cancer risk.

claims.sentence: Coils placed around the part of the body being studied help to send and receive the radio waves and improve the quality of the pictures.
claims.evidence: No retrieved text mentions coils.

claims.sentence: The person operating the scanner watches from another room.
claims.evidence: NHS: the radiographer controls the scanner from another room and can hear and speak to you.

claims.sentence: Scan length depends on the area examined, and NHS trust leaflets quote different times, from about 10 minutes to about 90 minutes.
claims.evidence: Retrieved NHS wording: 15 to 90 minutes depending on area and number of images; Gloucestershire leaflet gives image capture of about 10 to 45 minutes.

claims.sentence: One trust says the total time in the department is likely to be about an hour.
claims.evidence: Gloucestershire leaflet: total time in the department likely to be about 60 minutes.

claims.sentence: Staff settle the person on a couch that slides into the scanner.
claims.evidence: NHS: lie on a flat motorised bed that moves inside the scanner.

claims.sentence: An intercom lets the person talk to the radiographer, and a call button is provided.
claims.evidence: Intercom and monitor are supported (radiographer can see and speak to you); a call button was not found in retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: An intercom lets the person talk to the radiographer during the scan.

claims.sentence: The person is asked to keep still, because movement can blur the pictures.
claims.evidence: Trust leaflet: keep as still as possible to avoid blurry images.

claims.sentence: Some scans include an injection of contrast, a dye that helps to produce a more detailed picture and improves the accuracy of the scan.
claims.evidence: Gloucestershire leaflet: contrast medium injected via a cannula helps produce a more detailed image and improves accuracy.

claims.sentence: MedlinePlus says contrast is usually given through a vein, and that the most common agent contains gadolinium.
claims.evidence: MedlinePlus text was not retrieved. Only trial consent forms mention gadolinium given by vein, not a reputable source; NHS trust leaflets say contrast is injected into a vein via a cannula.
claims.newSentence: Some scans use contrast dye, which NHS trust leaflets say is injected into a vein through a small tube called a cannula.

claims.sentence: It adds that allergic reactions to this substance rarely occur.
claims.evidence: MedlinePlus text not retrieved. NHS Inform says complications are rare but some people get side effects or an allergic reaction to the contrast dye.
claims.newSentence: NHS Inform says complications are rare, but some people have side effects or an allergic reaction to the contrast dye.

claims.sentence: MedlinePlus also says gadolinium can be harmful for people with kidney problems who need dialysis, so kidney health is a standard question before a contrast scan.
claims.evidence: Kidney/dialysis statement came only from trial consent forms, not a reputable patient source; not retrieved from MedlinePlus.

claims.sentence: The scanner makes loud beeping or hammering noises, so earplugs or headphones are provided and some departments play music.
claims.evidence: NHS: the scanner is loud and ear protection is provided; music may be played or radio allowed.

claims.sentence: MedlinePlus notes that some people feel claustrophobic, which means anxious in enclosed spaces.
claims.evidence: MedlinePlus not retrieved. NHS says MRI is painless and safe but noisy and may create a feeling of claustrophobia.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says an MRI scan is noisy and may create a feeling of claustrophobia, which means feeling anxious in enclosed spaces.

claims.sentence: Trust leaflets say some people find the scan difficult for this reason.
claims.evidence: No retrieved leaflet text states that people find the scan difficult; claim is redundant with the NHS claustrophobia wording.

claims.sentence: They list options such as visiting the department beforehand, using a wider scanner, techniques that staff can use during the scan, or a mild sedative prescribed by a GP.
claims.evidence: Wide-bore benefit found in studies (PubMed), not leaflets; sedative via GP and pre-visit not found in retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: A study found that a wide-bore scanner increased the success rate of MRI in people with claustrophobia.

claims.sentence: A person who has a sedative needs someone to take them home afterwards.
claims.evidence: Trust leaflet: after a sedative a friend or relative will need to take you home and stay with you; not safe to drive for 24 hours.

claims.sentence: Before the scan each person completes a safety questionnaire.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: patients complete an MRI safety questionnaire; screening questionnaires are standard.

claims.sentence: York Hospitals says there are no known risks from an MRI scan when a person meets the safety standards.
claims.evidence: 'No known risks' not found; NHS describes MRI as painless and safe although noisy. 'No known risks' is an absolute safety claim.
claims.newSentence: The NHS describes MRI as painless and safe, although it is noisy.

claims.sentence: The magnet can make pacemakers, artificial limbs and other implanted devices that contain metal malfunction or heat up, according to MedlinePlus.
claims.evidence: NHS: strong magnet can pull strongly on some metals; people with a metal implant such as a pacemaker or artificial joint may not be able to have an MRI. MedlinePlus attribution and 'heat up' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says the MRI magnet is strong, so people with a metal implant such as a pacemaker or artificial joint may not be able to have a scan.

claims.sentence: Loose metal objects can be pulled toward the magnet and cause injury.
claims.evidence: Only paraphrased wording 'strong magnet can pull strongly on some metals' retrieved; MedlinePlus not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The magnet is strong enough to pull strongly on some metals.

claims.sentence: For that reason removable metal, such as jewellery and watches, comes off before the scan.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: patients asked to remove magnetic objects and change into a gown (trust leaflet); jewellery and watches not named in a reputable source.
claims.newSentence: NHS trust leaflets say patients are asked to remove magnetic objects and may change into a gown before the scan.

claims.sentence: Some implants, such as certain brain aneurysm clips or programmable shunts, may mean a scan cannot be done.
claims.evidence: Scottish NHS MRI physics pages: MR Conditional clips can be scanned only if conditions are met; programmable shunt valves are MR Conditional and may need resetting. 'Cannot be done' not stated generally.
claims.newSentence: NHS safety policies say some implants, such as aneurysm clips and programmable shunt valves, can be scanned only if specific conditions are met.

claims.sentence: Implants made of non-magnetic material are usually labelled MR safe or MR conditional, and some pacemakers can be scanned under strict conditions, according to a safety review.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: MR conditional pacemaker systems are available and scanning is allowed only under precautions; 'non-magnetic ... usually labelled MR safe' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Some implants, including some pacemakers, are labelled MR conditional, which means they can be scanned only under set conditions.

claims.sentence: Trust leaflets ask people to tell the imaging staff about any implants.
claims.evidence: NHS: important for the radiographer carrying out the scan to be aware of any metal in the body.

claims.sentence: MedlinePlus says tattoo dyes can irritate the skin or eyes, and medication patches can cause a skin burn.
claims.evidence: Tattoo dye and patch burns came only from trial consent forms, not a reputable patient source.

claims.sentence: Usually no preparation is needed, and people can typically eat and drink as normal.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: most MRI scans need no special preparation (NHS trust info). 'Eat and drink as normal' only found for prostate MRI.
claims.newSentence: Most MRI scans need no special preparation, according to NHS trust information.

claims.sentence: Some scans of the abdomen or pelvis may need fasting for a few hours, and bowel-relaxing medicine is sometimes given.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: fasting for some pelvis, gall bladder or small bowel scans (4 to 6 hours in trust leaflets); Buscopan bowel-relaxing injection used for abdominal and pelvic scans.

claims.sentence: Results are not usually given on the day of the scan.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: NHS 1 to 2 weeks; results usually discussed at a follow-up appointment.

claims.sentence: A radiologist, a doctor who specialises in reading scans, studies the images and writes a report for the doctor who requested the scan.
claims.evidence: Radiologist reads the images; report goes to the doctor who ordered the scan.

claims.sentence: That doctor then discusses the findings with the person.
claims.evidence: Report goes to the referring doctor; results discussed at follow-up appointment.

claims.sentence: The main extra risks come from the injection, as a small chance of a reaction to the contrast, and rare discomfort or tissue damage if the cannula, the small tube in the vein, leaks.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: complications rare; side effects or allergic reaction to the dye possible. Cannula leak not found.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says complications from an MRI scan are rare, but some people get side effects or an allergic reaction to the contrast dye.

claims.sentence: Trouble breathing or swelling of the face after an injection would need a 999 call.
claims.evidence: 999 instruction not found. Retrieved: reactions mostly happen soon after the dye, so people are often asked to wait about 30 minutes (trust leaflet).
claims.newSentence: Reactions to contrast dye usually happen soon after the injection, so some trusts ask people to stay for about 30 minutes afterwards.

claims.sentence: MRI uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to take detailed pictures, and it does not use X-rays.
claims.evidence: As claims 1, 2: magnet and radio waves, no X-rays; 'detailed' acceptable (contrast gives more detailed pictures).

claims.sentence: The scanner is loud, so earplugs or headphones are provided, and staff can talk to the person through an intercom.
claims.evidence: Ear protection provided and intercom contact retrieved (NHS).

claims.sentence: A safety questionnaire is completed first because some implanted devices can stop a scan from going ahead.
claims.evidence: Safety questionnaire standard; NHS says people with metal implants such as pacemakers may not be able to have MRI.

claims.sentence: Results are not usually given on the day: a radiologist reports the images to the doctor who requested the scan.
claims.evidence: Radiologist reads images; report goes to the requesting doctor; results not given on the day (1 to 2 weeks).

claims.sentence: An MRI scan uses a strong magnet and radio waves, not X-rays, to take detailed pictures. This guide covers noise, safety checks, contrast and results.
claims.evidence: Sentence 1 supported (magnet, radio waves, no X-rays); sentence 2 is a description of the guide's contents.

notes: Extra facts: (1) NHS says a radiographer controls the scanner from another room and can hear and speak to the person, and can see them on a monitor (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/mri-scan/what-happens/). (2) A trust leaflet says reactions to contrast mostly happen soon after, so some people wait about 30 minutes (https://www.nhsinform.scot/tests-and-treatments/scans-and-x-rays/mri-scan). (3) NHS Scotland MRI physics pages give implant-specific conditions for clips and shunts (https://www.mriphysics.scot.nhs.uk/implant-safety-policies/aneurysm-clips/). (4) Wide-bore scanners improved success in claustrophobic patients (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21598040/). MedlinePlus MRI page and the York/Barnsley/NBT leaflets were not directly retrieved, so all MedlinePlus-attributed sentences were reworded or removed. Search results arrive as summaries, not verbatim page text.
